newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe expected to announce tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: Juppe expected to announce tax reforms.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, keen to dispel pessimism about weak economic growth and high unemployment, will announce on Thursday government plans to cut income taxes over the next five years.
His office said Juppe would announce the plans to the French people at 2000 GMT. A government source said the announcement would probably be made on television.

The government has promised to cut at least 20 billion french francs ($3.93 billion) off income tax next year while Francois Leotard, president of France's UDF parliamentary party, said on Wednesday the government planned to cut income taxes by 75 billion francs over the next five years.
"The prime minister said the cut in income taxes would be 75 billion francs in five years," Leotard said after a meeting with Juppe.
In announcing the tax cuts, the government appears to be hoping to restore consumer confidence, lift consumer spending, and boost growth.

The French economy shrank by 0.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996, hit by a fall in consumer spending, after increasing 1.1 percent in the first quarter, national statistics institute INSEE said on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said in a radio interview "psychological factors" could play a role in fuelling the economic recovery.
"I have high hopes that the reduction in taxes to be contained in the 1997 budget bill and beyond will be able to act as the trigger," he said.
"It is like a football team. When the team believes it can do it, it scores goals. When it doubts itself it sometimes lets the opposition score," he said.

The government has insisted that despite current pessimism the economy is recovering. It is counting on a recovery to help it cut budget deficits in preparation for European monetary union and also appease a restive workforce anxious about new cuts in public spending.
